You won't know about me unless you've read a book called The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, but that doesn't matter. Mr. Mark Twain wrote that book, and he mostly told the truth. He exaggerated some things, but most of it was true. That's nothing unusual. I've never known anyone who didn't tell a lie now and then, except maybe Aunt Polly, or the widow, or Mary. Aunt Polly—that's Tom's Aunt Polly—and Mary and the Widow Douglas are all in that book. Like I said, it's mostly true, with a few tall tales mixed in.

Here's how that book ends: Tom and I found the money the robbers had hidden in the cave, and it made us rich. We each got six thousand dollars, all in gold. Piled up, it was a mighty lot of money to look at. Judge Thatcher took it and invested it, and the interest brought each of us a dollar a day all year long. That was more money than anyone could figure out how to spend. The Widow Douglas took me in as her son and said she would civilize me. But living indoors all the time was hard, especially with the widow being so terribly proper and regular in everything she did. When I couldn't stand it anymore, I ran off. I put on my old rags and went back to sleeping in my big sugar barrel, free and happy. But Tom Sawyer tracked me down and said he was starting a gang of robbers. I could join if I went back to the widow and made myself respectable. So I went back.

The widow cried over me and called me a poor lost lamb, along with plenty of other names, though she didn't mean any harm. She put me back into those new clothes. All I could do was sweat and feel squeezed in. Then the old business started again. The widow rang a bell for supper, and you had to turn up on time. At the table, you couldn't just start eating. You had to wait while she bowed her head and muttered over the food, although there wasn't anything wrong with it, except that every dish was cooked separately. It's different in a barrel of leftovers. Everything mixes together, the juices trade places, and the food tastes better.

After supper she brought out her book and taught me about Moses and the Bulrushers. I was eager to hear all about him, but after a while she let slip that Moses had been dead a very long time. Then I stopped caring, because dead people don't interest me.

Once this was done, I detached a few more loops from the rim, worked in another section of cloth, and fastened the loose loops to their corresponding buttons. In this way I could insert the entire upper portion of the bag between the netting and the hoop. Clearly the hoop would now fall inside the basket, leaving the buttons alone to support the full weight of the basket and everything it contained. At first this might seem an inadequate support, but it was nothing of the kind. The buttons were exceptionally strong and placed so closely together that each bore only a very small fraction of the total load. Indeed, I would have felt no concern even if the basket and its contents had weighed three times as much. I then lifted the hoop again inside the rubber covering and supported it at almost its previous height with three lightweight poles prepared for this purpose. Naturally, this kept the top of the bag spread open and held the lower part of the netting in its proper position. All that remained was to seal the opening of the enclosure. I easily accomplished this by gathering the folds of material together and twisting them tightly from inside with a sort of fixed tourniquet.

“Three circular panes of thick, clear glass had been fitted into the sides of the covering now surrounding the basket. These allowed me an unobstructed view in every horizontal direction. A fourth window of the same kind was set into the fabric beneath me, aligned with a small opening in the basket's floor. Through it I could look straight down. However, I had been unable to fit any similar arrangement overhead because of the particular way the upper opening was closed and the resulting folds in the cloth. I therefore could not expect to see anything directly above me. This scarcely mattered, of course: even if I had managed to install a window at the top, the balloon itself would have blocked the view and made it useless.

“About a foot beneath one of the side windows was a circular opening eight inches across. It was fitted with a brass rim whose inner edge was threaded to receive a screw. Into this rim I screwed the condenser's large tube, while the body of the machine remained, of course, inside the rubber chamber.

It was well past noon when he woke. His servant had tiptoed into the bedroom several times to see whether he was stirring, wondering why his young master was sleeping so late. At last the bell rang. Victor quietly brought in a cup of tea and a stack of letters on a small antique Sèvres china tray. He pulled back the olive satin curtains, lined with shimmering blue, from the three tall windows.

“Monsieur has slept well this morning,” he said with a smile.

“What time is it, Victor?” Dorian Gray asked sleepily.

“A quarter past one, Monsieur.”

So late! He sat up, drank a little tea, and looked through his letters. One was from Lord Henry and had been delivered by hand that morning. After a moment's hesitation, he set it aside. He opened the others without much interest. They held the usual cards, dinner invitations, tickets to private art viewings, charity concert programs, and similar things that arrived in fashionable young men's mail every morning during the social season. There was a large bill for an engraved silver grooming set in the Louis XV style. He had not yet dared to send it to his guardians. They were extremely old-fashioned and failed to understand that, in our age, unnecessary things are the only things we need. There were also several very polite letters from moneylenders in Jermyn Street, offering to lend any amount immediately at the most reasonable interest rates.

After about ten minutes he rose, put on an elaborate cashmere dressing gown embroidered with silk, and went into the bathroom with its onyx floor. The cool water refreshed him after his long sleep. He seemed to have forgotten everything he had been through. Once or twice he vaguely felt that he had taken part in some strange tragedy, but it seemed as unreal as a dream.

Once dressed, he entered the library and sat down to a light French breakfast on a small round table beside the open window. The day was beautiful. The warm air seemed full of spices. A bee flew inside and circled the bowl decorated with blue dragons that stood before him, filled with bright yellow roses. He felt completely happy.

Then he noticed the screen he had placed in front of the portrait and gave a start.

“Is Monsieur too cold?” his servant asked, setting an omelette on the table. “Shall I close the window?”

Dorian shook his head. “I'm not cold,” he murmured.
